Why bootstrap?

Source: vignettes/articles/why-bootstrap.Rmd
why-bootstrap.Rmd

Sensitivity analysis asks how strong an omitted variable would have to be to change a regression result. The most common answer in management research is the impact threshold of a confounding variable (ITCV; Frank, 2000): the smallest product of correlations with the predictor and with the outcome that an omitted variable needs to make a significant coefficient insignificant. sensemakr (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020) answers differently: it reports the coefficient you would have obtained had a variable as strong as an observed covariate been omitted, with a confidence interval.

Lonati and Wulff (2026) show that both answers rest on the conventional OLS variance formula. The ITCV is computed from a t statistic, and its reading as a product of correlations holds only when that t statistic is the conventional one. The confidence interval of sensemakr is derived under the same assumption. As soon as the regression calls for heteroskedasticity- or cluster-robust standard errors, which is the rule rather than the exception in organizational research, the ITCV remains computable but is no longer a product of correlations, and the analytic interval is wrong by the same factor as the conventional standard error. The remedy is to bootstrap sensemakr, as Cinelli, Ferwerda and Hazlett (2024, Appendix C) propose; bootmakr automates it.

This page shows the problem and the remedy on the package’s simulated data, in R and in Stata.

The example

firms is a simulated panel of 250 firms observed for 20 years. The true effect of x on y is 0.25. Two firm-level characteristics drive both x and y: an observed control c and a variable q that we leave out of the regression, as a researcher who does not have it would. The within-firm components of x and of the disturbance are persistent, so standard errors must be clustered by firm. Because the data are simulated, q is in the file and every verdict can be checked.

One coefficient, two standard errors

Estimate the regression that omits q, once with conventional and once with cluster-robust standard errors.

library(bootmakr)
library(sandwich)
data("firms")

fit <- lm(y ~ x + c, data = firms)

se <- c(conventional = sqrt(vcov(fit)["x", "x"]),
        clustered    = sqrt(vcovCL(fit, cluster = ~ firm)["x", "x"]))
round(c(estimate = coef(fit)[["x"]], se, ratio = se[["clustered"]] / se[["conventional"]]), 3)
#>     estimate conventional    clustered        ratio 
#>        0.445        0.014        0.041        2.984
use firms, clear
quietly regress y x c
lincom x

quietly regress y x c, vce(cluster firm)
lincom x
 ( 1)  x = 0

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
           y | Coefficient  Std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
         (1) |   .4445283    .013584    32.72   0.000     .4178977    .4711589
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 ( 1)  x = 0

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
           y | Coefficient  Std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
         (1) |   .4445283   .0405336    10.97   0.000      .364696    .5243607
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The coefficient is 0.44, well above the true 0.25, because q is omitted. The clustered standard error is 3.0 times the conventional one. Nothing about the coefficient changed; only the uncertainty attached to it did.

What the ITCV makes of it

The ITCV turns the t statistic of the coefficient into a t-implied correlation, t / √(t² + df), does the same for the critical t, and reports the gap between the two, rescaled so that it reads as the product of correlations an omitted variable would need to close it. Here it is for both t statistics. (The code implements the definition directly; the konfound package for R gives the same numbers.)

t.conv <- coef(fit)[["x"]] / se[["conventional"]]
t.clus <- coef(fit)[["x"]] / se[["clustered"]]
df <- fit$df.residual

itcv <- function(t, df) {
  r.implied  <- t / sqrt(t^2 + df)             # the t-implied correlation
  t.crit     <- qt(0.975, df)
  r.critical <- t.crit / sqrt(t.crit^2 + df)
  c(r_implied = r.implied, ITCV = (r.implied - r.critical) / (1 - abs(r.critical)))
}
round(rbind(conventional = itcv(t.conv, df), clustered = itcv(t.clus, df)), 3)
#>              r_implied  ITCV
#> conventional     0.420 0.404
#> clustered        0.153 0.129
quietly regress y x c
scalar t_conv = _b[x] / _se[x]
scalar df = e(df_r)
quietly regress y x c, vce(cluster firm)
scalar t_rob = _b[x] / _se[x]

* the ITCV: t-implied correlation minus the critical one (Frank, 2000)
scalar r_crit = invttail(df, .025) / sqrt(invttail(df, .025)^2 + df)
foreach v in conv rob {
    scalar r_impl_`v' = t_`v' / sqrt(t_`v'^2 + df)
    scalar itcv_`v' = (r_impl_`v' - r_crit) / (1 - abs(r_crit))
}
display "conventional SE: t-implied correlation = " %5.3f r_impl_conv ///
    "   ITCV = " %5.3f itcv_conv
display "clustered SE:    t-implied correlation = " %5.3f r_impl_rob ///
    "   ITCV = " %5.3f itcv_rob "   sqrt(ITCV) = " %5.3f sqrt(itcv_rob)
conventional SE: t-implied correlation = 0.420   ITCV = 0.404

clustered SE:    t-implied correlation = 0.153   ITCV = 0.129   sqrt(ITCV) = 0.359

With conventional standard errors the ITCV is .40; with clustered ones it drops to .13. Read as a product of correlations, the second number says that an omitted variable correlated about .36 with both x and y (the square root of the ITCV) would be enough to overturn the result. Now look at q, whose correlations we know. The ITCV computed above is its conditional form, stated in partial correlations given the other covariates, so we take q’s partial correlations given c.

partial <- function(a, b) {
  cor(resid(lm(firms[[a]] ~ firms$c)), resid(lm(firms[[b]] ~ firms$c)))
}
round(c(q_with_x = partial("q", "x"), q_with_y = partial("q", "y"),
        impact = partial("q", "x") * partial("q", "y"),
        x_with_y = partial("x", "y")), 3)
#> q_with_x q_with_y   impact x_with_y 
#>    0.468    0.537    0.251    0.420
* partial correlations given c, by residualising on c
foreach v in x y q {
    quietly regress `v' c
    predict double `v'_c, resid
}
quietly correlate x_c y_c
scalar r_xy_c = r(rho)
quietly correlate x_c q_c
scalar r_xq_c = r(rho)
quietly correlate y_c q_c
scalar r_yq_c = r(rho)
display "partial correlation of x and y given c: " %5.3f r_xy_c
display "q with x given c: " %5.3f r_xq_c "   q with y given c: " %5.3f r_yq_c ///
    "   impact of q: " %5.3f r_xq_c * r_yq_c
partial correlation of x and y given c: 0.420

q with x given c: 0.468   q with y given c: 0.537   impact of q: 0.251

The impact of q is .25. That is below the conventional ITCV (.40), so the conventional ITCV says that q is not strong enough to overturn the result. It is above the clustered ITCV (.13), so the clustered ITCV says that q is strong enough. One of them must be wrong, and we can find out which: put q into the regression.

fit.q <- lm(y ~ x + c + q, data = firms)
round(c(estimate = coef(fit.q)[["x"]],
        se_conventional = sqrt(vcov(fit.q)["x", "x"]),
        se_clustered    = sqrt(vcovCL(fit.q, cluster = ~ firm)["x", "x"])), 3)
#>        estimate se_conventional    se_clustered 
#>           0.229           0.014           0.037
regress y x c q, vce(cluster firm)
Linear regression                               Number of obs     =      5,000
                                                F(3, 249)         =     199.21
                                                Prob > F          =     0.0000
                                                R-squared         =     0.4785
                                                Root MSE          =     .99577

                                 (Std. err. adjusted for 250 clusters in firm)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |               Robust
           y | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
           x |   .2286068    .036788     6.21   0.000     .1561516    .3010621
           c |    .578841   .0492042    11.76   0.000     .4819316    .6757504
           q |   .5125708   .0486366    10.54   0.000     .4167793    .6083623
       _cons |   .0400548   .0455783     0.88   0.380    -.0497133    .1298229
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

With q in the model the coefficient of x is 0.23, close to the true 0.25, with a clustered standard error of 0.037: it remains clearly different from zero. The clustered ITCV was wrong. Its reading as a product of correlations fails because the t-implied correlation it is built on, .15, is not the correlation between x and y given c, which is .42. With conventional standard errors the two coincide (.42); that coincidence is what the ITCV derivation uses. With robust standard errors the t-implied correlation equals the actual correlation divided by √(ratio² (1 − r²) + r²), where ratio is the robust standard error over the conventional one (Lonati & Wulff, 2026, Equation 4). When robust standard errors are larger than conventional ones, the usual case, the ITCV overstates the threat from omitted variables; when they are smaller, it understates it. There is no “correct ITCV” to be had under robust inference: two omitted variables with the same correlations can change a robust standard error in different ways, so no product of correlations corresponds to the robust t statistic. Degrees-of-freedom corrections, fixed effects and feasible generalized least squares do not repair this; the paper goes through each of them.

Analytic sensemakr has the same problem

sensemakr does not need the ITCV. For an omitted variable as strong as c, it computes the bias-adjusted coefficient directly, and that estimate is a function of the data alone. But the standard error and confidence interval it attaches to the adjusted coefficient are derived under conventional OLS inference (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020).

sensemakr::ovb_bounds(fit, treatment = "x", benchmark_covariates = "c", kd = 1)[
  , c("bound_label", "adjusted_estimate", "adjusted_se", "adjusted_lower_CI", "adjusted_upper_CI")]
#>   bound_label adjusted_estimate adjusted_se adjusted_lower_CI adjusted_upper_CI
#> 1        1x c         0.2521337  0.01331711         0.2260263         0.2782411
sensemakr y x c, treat(x) benchmark(c) kd(1)
                                                            DOF    =    4997
                                                            q      =    1.00
                                                            alpha  =    0.05
                                                            reduce =    TRUE
                                                            H0     =       0

 Treatment      |     Coef.      S.E.      t(H0)    R2yd.x     RV_q    RV_qa
----------------+-----------------------------------------------------------
              x |    0.4445    0.0136    32.7244    0.1765   0.3680   0.3507

 1.00x               c |   0.1673    1.0000    0.0141

The adjusted estimate, 0.252, is close to the coefficient with q in the model. Its analytic standard error, 0.013, is close to the conventional standard error of that coefficient (0.014) and far below the clustered one (0.037). The analytic interval, from 0.226 to 0.278, is therefore about 2.8 times too narrow in these data, for exactly the reason the ITCV fails: a formula built on the conventional variance is being applied to a regression that needs a robust one.

What the bootstrap does

Cinelli, Ferwerda and Hazlett (2024, Appendix C) propose to replace the analytic interval by a bootstrap: resample the data the way you would choose standard errors (observations for heteroskedasticity, whole clusters for clustered data), refit the regression and recompute the adjusted estimate in every replication, and take the percentiles of the resulting distribution as the confidence interval. bootmakr does this in one call.

boot <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                 benchmark_covariates = "c", cluster = "firm",
                 seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
boot
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x", benchmark_covariates = "c", 
#>     seed = 123, cluster = "firm", progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (1,000 reps, n = 5,000, 250 clusters)
#> Benchmark: c | kd = 1, ky = 1
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (percentile 95% CI):
#>   Estimate Std. Err     2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)  
#> x 0.252134 0.076236 0.087365 0.394215     0.01 *
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; CI and p-value from percentile bootstrap)
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                       Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> c with treatment | X      0.1433       0.379
#> c with outcome | D, X     0.1248       0.353
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>           kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx Impact
#> 1.00x c 1.00 1.00 0.1673  0.1998  0.222
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates. Impact: product of
#>  its partial correlations with the outcome and with the treatment, both given the
#>  covariates only, i.e. the scale of the ITCV; signed so that the omitted variable
#>  biases the estimate away from zero. Descriptive only: independent of the variance
#>  estimator, and not a threshold.)
bootmakr y x c, treat(x) benchmark(c) cluster(firm) seed(123)

The adjusted estimate is the same as before. Its bootstrap standard error is 0.076 (0.074 in Stata, which draws different random numbers), and the percentile interval runs from 0.09 to 0.39. The interval is wider than the clustered interval of the regression that includes q, for two reasons. One is the reason this page is about: the bootstrap, resampling firms, reflects the clustered uncertainty of the coefficient, not the conventional one. The other is that in every replication the strength of the benchmark c is re-estimated too, so the interval also carries the uncertainty about how strong “as strong as c” is. The paper’s own example (Table 2 of Lonati & Wulff, 2026) separates the two by giving sensemakr the omitted variable’s strength directly, which the R package allows:

manual <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                   r2dz.x  = partial("q", "x")^2,
                   r2yz.dx = sensemakr::partial_r2(fit.q, covariates = "q"),
                   cluster = "firm", seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
manual$results[, c("estimate", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "pvalue")]
#>    estimate         se  ci_lower  ci_upper pvalue
#> 1 0.2286068 0.04087705 0.1511528 0.3088602      0

With q’s actual strength, the bootstrap standard error is 0.041, next to the clustered standard error of 0.037 that the regression with q gives: the bootstrap recovers the inference that would have been obtained had q been observed, as it does in the paper. (The sensemakr command on SSC does not accept a strength given by hand, so this step has no Stata counterpart.)

The resampling scheme is what makes the bootstrap robust, and it is your choice. Resampling observations instead of firms gives

rows <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                 benchmark_covariates = "c",
                 seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
rows$results[, c("estimate", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")]
#>    estimate         se ci_lower ci_upper
#> 1 0.2521337 0.02115902 0.211228 0.295048
quietly bootmakr y x c, treat(x) benchmark(c) seed(123)
display "observations resampled:  SE = " %6.4f r(se) ///
    "   95% CI [" %6.4f r(ci_lower) ", " %6.4f r(ci_upper) "]"
observations resampled:  SE = 0.0216   95% CI [0.2078, 0.2937]

a standard error of 0.021, too small by the same factor as the conventional standard error, because observations of the same firm are treated as independent. Resample the units you would cluster on; see Clustered and stratified data.

In the paper

Lonati and Wulff (2026) make this argument formally, illustrate it with a simulated example like the one above (without c, and with a stronger q), and test bootstrap-based sensemakr against the ITCV in a Monte Carlo study with heteroskedastic, clustered, unbalanced and weak-benchmark designs. The bootstrap interval comes close to nominal coverage in most conditions, far closer than the analytic interval, while the ITCV’s mistakes grow with the sample size under clustering. The paper ends with a four-stage workflow (which standard errors, how different are they, how strong is a plausible omitted variable, can the bootstrap be trusted) that the worked example follows on a published study.

References

Cinelli, C., & Hazlett, C. (2020). Making sense of sensitivity: Extending omitted variable bias. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 82(1), 39–67. https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12348

Cinelli, C., Ferwerda, J., & Hazlett, C. (2024). sensemakr: Sensitivity analysis tools for OLS in R and Stata. Observational Studies, 10(2), 93–127. https://doi.org/10.1353/obs.2024.a946583

Frank, K. A. (2000). Impact of a confounding variable on a regression coefficient. Sociological Methods & Research, 29(2), 147–194. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124100029002001

Lonati, S., & Wulff, J. N. (2026). Why you should not use the ITCV with robust standard errors (and what to do instead). Academy of Management Proceedings, 2026(1). https://doi.org/10.5465/AMPROC.2026.247bp
